reader_question: Which federal court hears a case from my state, and where does an appeal go?
grade_line: Documented: the text of title 28 of the U.S. Code, as in force on November 12, 2026, with the territorial courts from title 48
title: The 94 district courts try federal cases, an appeal goes to the court of appeals for the region, and the Supreme Court sits over all 13 courts of appeals.
measure_line: The Supreme Court, the 13 courts of appeals and the 94 district courts, with the judgeships the law authorizes for each, as the 2024 edition of the U.S. Code sets them, retrieved November 12, 2026
notes: The law authorizes 179 judgeships on the courts of appeals, 673 in the district courts of the states, DC and Puerto Rico, a few of them shared between districts of one state, and four in the territorial courts of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the Virgin Islands, whose judges serve 10-year terms. Judges of the Article III courts, the courts the Constitution’s Article III sets up, hold their seats for life.
Judgeships count the seats the law creates, filled or vacant, and leave out senior judges.
alt: A tree of the federal courts. The Supreme Court, with nine justices, sits at the top. Under it are 12 regional courts of appeals, from the District of Columbia Circuit with 11 judgeships to the Ninth Circuit with 29, each listing the states and territories whose district courts it hears appeals from, with each district court’s judgeships; the Ninth Circuit’s districts hold the most, 112. Apart from them, the Federal Circuit, with 12 judgeships, hears appeals by subject from every district. The courts of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the Virgin Islands are territorial courts, not Article III courts.
